indices.description:
Labels for elements along ndarray axes.
For example, for a three-dimensional ndarray with sources in the first dimension, dates in the second, and metrics
in the third, indices.get(0)[j] would be the label for the j-th source, indices.get(1)[j] would be the label for
the j-th date, and indices.get(2)[j] would be the label for j-th metric.

Each string array can contain null, indicating that there is no label at that particular position.

**CAUTION**: We recommend not to use the range delimiter ":" in a label.  This may be confused by the parser used
by the underlying implementation of various functions. For example, see {@link AbstractTensor#subTensor}.

shape.description:
The shape of the n-dimensional array.
For example, a 3x10x6 array should have shape [3, 10, 6].
Note: if an {@link NdArrayStream} has an infinite or unknown (too expensive to calculate) iteration length,
then the first dimension will have length -1.

axes.description:
Labels for array dimensions themselves.
For example, for a three-dimensional array with sources in the first dimension, dates in the second, and metrics
in the third, axes could be ["source", "timestamp", "expression"].

sourceDimension.description:
The dimension (0-indexed) of the tensor that contains the "sources" of the tensor's data.
NOTE: this field is not respected when streaming data, which assumes the first dimension
as the indexing dimension. As an example, see {@link AbstractTensor#isStoredByReference}.

flattenedData.description:
All of the data in the tensor flattened into a 1-D array.

Data points are ordered in C-memory ordering, i.e. with the last dimension being the most rapidly changing
dimension.
E.g. For a 2-D Tensor, if first dimension is time and second dimension is metric, then
data = [time0, time1, time2...] where timeX = [metric0, metric1, metric2, ...] at time X.
